quizzes.title: Tribunals and Ordinary Courts
quizzes.passage: Tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies whose basic aim is to adjudicate specialised disputes and to reduce the workload of constitutional courts. They operate in areas such as taxation, company law, environment, telecommunications, armed forces and administrative matters. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, established in 1941, is described as the first tribunal in India, and it was set up to reduce court workload, expedite adjudication of disputes and build expertise on tax matters. The Lok Sabha has passed the Tribunals Reforms Bill 2026, which seeks to establish a National Tribunals Commission for unified tribunal governance. The Bill is meant to replace the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021. The proposed commission would handle the selection of tribunal chairpersons and members, performance review of members, oversight of complaints and administrative supervision. Tribunal decisions remain subject to scrutiny by the concerned High Court. The National Green Tribunal aims at giving relief and compensation for environmental damage, and it works on the polluter pays principle and sustainable development. It hears civil cases under seven laws and is guided by the principles of natural justice. Its decisions can be executed as a decree of a civil court. The Bill also proposes a national tribunals data grid, which is one of the commission's major functions.

questions.q: According to the booklet, what kind of body is an Administrative Tribunal?
options: A court established directly by the Constitution
A branch of a High Court
An agency created by statute that derives its powers from the State
questions.explanation: The booklet describes an Administrative Tribunal as an agency created by statute that derives its powers from the State.

questions.q: Which quality is described as a crucial requirement for judges in a court of law?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that impartiality is a crucial requirement for judges in a court of law.

questions.q: Civil courts possess judicial authority over which category of suits?
options: Suits of a criminal nature only
Suits of a civil nature, unless barred by law
questions.explanation: Civil courts have judicial authority over suits of a civil nature unless a law bars them.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An Administrative Tribunal may be a party to a dispute that it decides.
Reason (R): Tribunals have power to try special cases defined by Statutes.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but the power to try special cases does not explain why a tribunal may be a party to a dispute.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Judges in ordinary courts   ->   A. Expert in administrative matters
II. Administrative Tribunal members   ->   D. Independent regarding tenure, terms and conditions of service
III. Presiding officer of a court   ->   B. Entirely controlled by the Executive
IV. Tribunal President or member   ->   C. Required to be trained in law
questions.explanation: Judges in ordinary courts are independent in tenure, tribunal members' tenure is controlled by the Executive, the presiding officer must be trained in law, and a tribunal President or member may be an administrative expert.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about courts and tribunals:
I. Tribunals have power to try special cases defined by Statutes.
II. The tenure of Administrative Tribunal members is controlled by the judiciary.
III. A President or Member of a tribunal must always be legally trained.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Only statement I is correct, since tribunal members' tenure is controlled by the Executive and legal training is not always required.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about courts and tribunals:
1. Judges in ordinary courts are independent regarding tenure, terms and conditions of service.
2. Impartiality is not a requirement for judges in a court of law.
3. Civil courts have judicial authority over all suits, including those barred by law.
How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Only statement 1 is correct, because impartiality is a crucial requirement and civil courts' authority excludes suits barred by law.

quizzes.passage: The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, established in 1941, is described as the first tribunal in India. It was set up to reduce court workload, expedite adjudication of disputes and build expertise on tax matters. Tribunals in general aim to adjudicate specialised disputes, and they operate in fields such as taxation, company law, environment and telecommunications. The Lok Sabha has passed the Tribunals Reforms Bill 2026 to establish a National Tribunals Commission for unified tribunal governance. The Bill seeks to replace the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 and to re-enact provisions that were struck down. Its framework aims at a common institutional structure for tribunals, with a national tribunals data grid among its functions. The National Green Tribunal aims at relief and compensation for environmental damage, and its work rests on the polluter pays principle and on sustainable development. It hears civil cases under seven laws and is guided by the principles of natural justice. Its decisions can be executed as a decree of a civil court, and tribunal decisions in general remain subject to scrutiny by the concerned High Court. The Supreme Court's role is reflected in Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2010-2025), which repeatedly scrutinised certain provisions relating to tribunals.

questions.q: Who entirely controls the tenure and conditions of service of Administrative Tribunal members? (one word)
questions.explanation: The booklet states that tribunal members' tenure and conditions are entirely controlled by the Executive (Government).

questions.q: Which quality is described as a crucial requirement for judges in a court of law? (one word)
questions.explanation: The booklet calls impartiality a crucial requirement for judges in a court of law.

questions.q: Tribunals have power to try special cases defined by which legal instrument? (one word)
questions.explanation: Tribunals have power to try special cases defined by Statutes.

questions.q: Civil courts have judicial authority over suits of a civil nature, unless what? (one word)
questions.explanation: Civil courts have judicial authority over civil suits unless barred by law.

questions.q: How does the booklet classify tribunals by type? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists the type of tribunals as quasi-judicial bodies.

questions.q: A tribunal President or member may not be legally trained but may be an expert in which field? (one word)
questions.explanation: A tribunal President or member may be an expert in administrative matters even without legal training.

questions.q: What word describes judges of ordinary courts regarding their tenure, terms and conditions of service? (one word)
questions.explanation: Judges in ordinary courts are independent regarding tenure, terms and conditions of service.

quizzes.title: Constitutional Framework for Tribunals
quizzes.passage: Tribunals in India are bodies that adjudicate specialised disputes, and they are meant to reduce the workload of constitutional courts. Their work spans many fields, including taxation, company law, environment, telecommunications, armed forces and administrative matters. Tribunal decisions remain subject to scrutiny by the concerned High Court. The National Green Tribunal aims at giving relief and compensation for environmental damage, and it works on the polluter pays principle and sustainable development. It hears civil cases under seven laws and is guided by the principles of natural justice. Its decisions can be executed as a decree of a civil court. The Lok Sabha has passed the Tribunals Reforms Bill 2026, which seeks to establish a National Tribunals Commission for unified tribunal governance. The Bill seeks to replace the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021, and it deals with the selection of tribunal chairpersons and members, performance review of members and maintaining a national tribunals data grid. The Supreme Court's role is reflected in Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2010-2025), which repeatedly scrutinised certain provisions relating to tribunals. Such scrutiny has focused on provisions that give the Executive excessive control over tribunals. The Bill also contains the re-enactment of provisions that were struck down earlier.

questions.q: Which amendment inserted Part XIV-A into the Constitution?
questions.explanation: Part XIV-A was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

questions.q: Which pair of Articles is contained in Part XIV-A?
questions.explanation: Part XIV-A contains Articles 323A and 323B, which deal with tribunals.

questions.q: In L. Chandra Kumar vs Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court held that judicial review under Articles 226/227 and Article 32 is part of which feature of the Constitution?
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court held that judicial review under Articles 226/227 and Article 32 is part of the Basic Structure.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Article 323A allows State Legislatures to establish Administrative Tribunals.
Reason (R): Article 323B allows Parliament or State Legislatures to establish tribunals for specified matters.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Article 323A empowers Parliament alone, so A is false, while Article 323B covers Parliament or State Legislatures for specified matters, so R is true.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Income Tax Appellate Tribunal   ->   A. Judicial review is part of the Basic Structure
II. First Administrative Reforms Commission   ->   D. Parliament or State Legislatures may set up tribunals for specified matters
III. L. Chandra Kumar case   ->   C. First tribunal in India, established in 1941
IV. Article 323B   ->   B. Recommended Civil Services Tribunals
questions.explanation: The ITAT was established in 1941, the Chandra Kumar case held judicial review part of the Basic Structure, the First ARC recommended Civil Services Tribunals, and Article 323B covers Parliament or State Legislatures.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the constitutional framework for tribunals:
I. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal was the first tribunal in India.
II. Article 323A allows State Legislatures to establish Administrative Tribunals.
III. Tribunal decisions are not subject to any scrutiny by the concerned High Court.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Only statement I is correct, since Article 323A gives the power to Parliament alone and tribunal decisions remain subject to High Court scrutiny.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Constitution's tribunal provisions:
1. Part XIV-A contains Articles 323A and 323B.
2. The First Administrative Reforms Commission recommended Civil Services Tribunals at national and state levels.
3. Judicial review under Articles 226/227 is not part of the Basic Structure.
How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, while statement 3 is wrong because the Supreme Court held judicial review is part of the Basic Structure.

questions.q: In which year was Part XIV-A inserted into the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment? (year)
questions.explanation: Part XIV-A was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

questions.q: Which Part of the Constitution, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, contains the provisions for setting up tribunals? (Part name)
questions.explanation: Part XIV-A of the Constitution contains Articles 323A and 323B.

questions.q: Which Article empowers Parliament alone to establish Administrative Tribunals? (article number)
questions.explanation: Article 323A empowers Parliament alone to establish Administrative Tribunals.

questions.q: Which case decided in 1997 held that judicial review under Articles 226/227 and Article 32 is part of the Basic Structure? (name of the first party)
questions.explanation: The L. Chandra Kumar vs Union of India judgment of 1997 made this holding.

questions.q: Which body recommended Civil Services Tribunals at the national and state levels? (name or abbreviation)
questions.explanation: The First Administrative Reforms Commission recommended Civil Services Tribunals for national and state levels.

questions.q: Apart from Parliament, which bodies can establish tribunals under Article 323B? (two words)
questions.explanation: Under Article 323B, Parliament and State Legislatures can both establish tribunals.

questions.q: Article 323B allows tribunals to be set up for which kind of matters? (one word)
questions.explanation: Article 323B allows tribunals to be set up for specified matters.
